articles.title: Cloud identity platform retires legacy authentication for privileged roles
articles.author: priya-raman
articles.summary: Privileged administrator roles will no longer be able to use legacy authentication protocols.

brief.what: Privileged administrator roles will no longer be able to use legacy authentication protocols.

brief.why: Scripts and older tools that use basic authentication will stop working for affected accounts.
brief.next: The provider has published a timeline and migration guidance.

articles.whyItMatters: Scripts and older tools that use basic authentication will stop working for affected accounts. Audit sign-in logs for legacy protocols and migrate automation to modern authentication or workload identities.

sections.heading: Summary
paragraphs: Privileged administrator roles will no longer be able to use legacy authentication protocols.
The change blocks protocols that cannot enforce multi-factor authentication.

sections.heading: Technical Analysis
paragraphs: Legacy authentication protocols cannot enforce multi-factor authentication and remain a common attack path.
Retiring them for privileged roles closes a class of password-spray and credential-stuffing attacks.

sections.heading: Impact
paragraphs: Scripts and older tools that use basic authentication will stop working for affected accounts.
Scripts and tools using basic authentication for admin tasks will stop working.

sections.heading: What you should know
paragraphs: Audit sign-in logs for legacy protocols and migrate automation to modern authentication or workload identities.
The provider has published a timeline and migration guidance.

articles.author: priya-raman
articles.summary: Devices that cannot run agents can now be enrolled into zero trust policy at the network level.
articles.imageAlt: Editorial illustration for cloud story: Cloudflare

brief.what: Devices that cannot run agents can now be enrolled into zero trust policy at the network level.
brief.who: Organisations with many headless devices in branches gain consistent policy.
brief.why: Organisations with many headless devices on branch networks gain more consistent policy enforcement.
brief.next: The feature requires a supported branch connector.

articles.whyItMatters: Organisations with many headless devices on branch networks gain more consistent policy enforcement. Inventory IoT devices, group them by function and apply least-privilege egress policies.

sections.heading: Summary
paragraphs: Devices that cannot run agents can now be enrolled into zero trust policy at the network level.
Policies are applied based on device groups rather than user identity.

sections.heading: Technical Analysis
paragraphs: Zero trust gateways inspect and control traffic based on identity and device posture rather than network location.
Unmanaged IoT devices cannot run agents, so they require network-level enrolment instead.

sections.heading: Impact
paragraphs: Organisations with many headless devices on branch networks gain more consistent policy enforcement.
Organisations with many headless devices in branches gain consistent policy.

sections.heading: What you should know
paragraphs: Inventory IoT devices, group them by function and apply least-privilege egress policies.
The feature requires a supported branch connector.
